phonemes.desc: the stressed opening syllable: short e bearing the acute accent — in the living accent system, a raised musical pitch rather than a heavy stress
trilled or tapped rhōtic r, short i, final voiceless s

pronunciation.approximation: 'EH-riss' — two quick syllables with the high note forward; nothing like the English slurring of 'heiress' or 'Eris' rhymed with 'ferrous'

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: ἔρις (eris), 'strife, quarrel, rivalry' — the goddess is the common noun made flesh, like Kháos or Némēsis

kin.label: PIE
kin.form: uncertain; older scholarship tied it to ὀρίνω (orínō), 'to stir, rouse', but Beekes judges the formation non-Indo-European — a Pre-Greek inheritance, fitting for a daughter of Night

pronunciation.note: Tier 2, accent-preserving. Ἔρις carries the acute accent on a short initial vowel but no long vowel (η/ω) and no circumflex; the restoration Éris preserves exactly one feature the ASCII 'Eris' loses — the stress — and so the temple stands at Tier 2.

domains.title: The Uninvited
domains.subtitle: Goddess of Strife and Discord — the quarrel that topples kingdoms and the rivalry that builds them
domains.lead: Éris is strife personified — the quarrel, the feud, the rivalry Greeks both cursed and quietly praised. Born of Nyx, Night herself, she was never asked to the feast and therefore changed the world. Hesiod insists there are two Erises: the hateful one who sows war, and the better one who stirs even the idle to work.

cards.name: The Golden Apple
cards.desc: Uninvited to the wedding of Peleus and Thetis, she rolls the golden apple ‘for the fairest’ — the first cause of the Trojan War (Cypria).

cards.name: The Two Erises
cards.desc: Hesiod separates the hateful Strife from her elder sister, the good Eris who stirs idle men to work (Works and Days 11–26).

cards.name: The War-Stirrer
cards.desc: In the Iliad she walks the battle small at first, her head striking the sky as she delights in the din (Iliad 4.440–443).

cards.name: Daughter of Night
cards.desc: The Theogony (224–232) makes her a motherless child of Nyx, who then bears her own brood of calamities without any father.

symbols.name: The Golden Apple
symbols.meaning: The apple of the Hesperides that Éris rolled among the wedding guests of Peleus and Thetis; the Cypria tradition (preserved in Proclus' summary) makes it the seed of the Trojan War — a single piece of fruit as the first cause of the greatest war in Greek memory.

symbols.name: The Inscription 'Kallistēi'
symbols.meaning: 'For the fairest' (τῇ καλλίστῃ) — the words cut into the apple itself. The inscription, not the fruit, is the weapon: a superlative with three claimants is a quarrel engineered in miniature.

symbols.name: Viper-Tressed Hair
symbols.meaning: Virgil gives the Roman Discordia serpent-entwined locks bound with blood-drenched fillets (Aeneid 6.280, 'Discordia demens, vipereum crinem vittis innexa cruentis'), kin to the Furies — strife wearing the visual grammar of vengeance.

symbols.name: The Swelling Stature
symbols.meaning: In Iliad 4 (440–445) Éris is 'small at first, but then she fixes her head in heaven while her feet walk the earth' — her growing body is her emblem: discord is always born tiny.

symbols.name: Place beside Árēs
symbols.meaning: Homer calls her 'sister and companion of man-slaying Ares' (Iliad 4.441), and on the shield of Achilles she strides through battle beside Tumult and Doom, clutching the wounded and the dead (Iliad 18.535–540). Her attribute is her company.

mythology.lead: Éris has no temples and almost no cult — her mythology is her meaning. Every surviving story is an anatomy of strife itself: where it comes from, whom it feeds, and how it grows from a whisper into a thing with its head in heaven.

myths.title: Born of Night, Mother of Calamities
myths.text: In the Theogony (224–232) Hesiod makes Éris a child of Nyx, Night, who bears her without a father among the other dark abstractions — Death, Sleep, Blame, Woe, the Hesperides, the Moirai. Éris then breeds her own terrible brood, the Kakodaimones: Toil, Forgetfulness, Famine, Pains, Combats, Battles, Murders, Manslaughters, Quarrels, Lies, Disputes, Lawlessness, Ruin (Atē), and Oath — and Oath, Hesiod adds, troubling most of all, ‘brings the most pain to men on earth when anyone swears falsely knowing it’. The genealogy is a single claim stated as a family tree: from one quarrel, every misery descends. It also fixes Éris’s cosmological position — she is not one of the stormy passions that trouble the daylight gods but a permanent resident of the dark, born of the Night that was there before anything else, including the quarrel between heaven and earth.

myths.title: Hesiod's Correction
myths.text: The Works and Days (11–26) opens by amending the poet's own Theogony: 'there was not one kind of Strife after all — on earth there are two.' The first, the elder, men blame, for she 'fosters evil war and slaughter'. The second, whom Zeus set in the roots of the earth, is much better for mortals: she rouses even the shiftless to work, for 'potter rivals potter, carpenter carpenter; beggar envies beggar, and poet poet'. Here Éris is split in two — envy as destroyer and emulation as the engine of all human striving — one of the earliest pieces of moral reflection in Greek literature. The passage matters beyond theology: it is the first time a Greek writer argues with himself in print, correcting a genealogy because experience demanded it.

myths.title: The Apple of Discord
myths.text: At the wedding of Peleus and Thetis, all the gods were feasted — except Éris, whose very nature barred her from the invitation list. The Cypria, as summarized in Proclus' Chrestomathy, tells that she came anyway and threw among the guests a golden apple 'to be a prize of beauty', inscribed kallistēi — 'for the fairest'. Hēra, Athēnâ, and Aphrodítē each claimed it; the dispute was sent for judgment to Paris on Mount Ida, and from that judgment, Proclus says flatly, came the Trojan War. Hyginus (Fabulae 92) retells the same scene. It is the founding myth of discord: exclusion breeds the quarrel that topples a kingdom. The wedding meant to bind heaven's new order together became the place where it split, and the instrument was not malice but a superlative — the mere existence of 'fairest' among three proud goddesses.

myths.title: Small at First, Then Filling the Sky
myths.text: Homer's most haunting personification of war comes in Iliad 4 (440–445), as the two armies close: among them walks Éris, 'the sister and companion of man-slaying Ares — she rears only a small crest at first, but then she fixes her head in the heavens while her feet walk the earth', hurling bitterness into the midst of both hosts. She reappears on the shield of Achilles (Iliad 18.535–540), bloody-robed among the wounded and the dead. The image is precise and it has never stopped being true: discord begins as a murmur and ends with its head in the clouds — and once she stands, no god can pull her down. That Homer gives the abstraction a growth spurt, and lets her delight in the din, shows the Greeks watching strife the way one watches weather: not as sin but as force.

lore.syncretism: Rome adopted her as Discordia, and the Roman poets made her darker still. Ennius opened his account of the outbreak of the Second Punic War with her: 'Discordia taetra belli ferratos postis portasque refregit' — 'when foul Discord burst the iron-bound posts and gates of war' (Annales, fr. 225 Skutsch), an image Virgil deliberately echoes at the underworld's entrance in Aeneid 6.280, where Discordia demens stands with viper-entwined, blood-bound hair. She never acquired the civic cult that other translations did — Rome, like Greece, preferred to name strife rather than worship it. Her modern afterlife is stranger and more literal than most: the Discordian movement of the 1960s made her its patroness, and in 2006 the dwarf planet whose discovery provoked the reclassification of Pluto was formally named Eris — a fitting tribute, the IAU noted, to the goddess of strife and discord.
lore.culturalLegacy: Her Roman name survives everywhere in English: discord, discordant, discordance, and the idiom 'apple of discord' for the object of a quarrel — a phrase that walked straight out of the Cypria into the modern tongues of Europe. Discordianism's Principia Discordia canonized her as the counter-goddess of an orderly world, and the dwarf planet Eris carries her name in every astronomy textbook, so the 'tenth planet' that demoted Pluto keeps her quarrel alive in the heavens. Among the Olympian circle she remains what she always was: the goddess nobody worships and everybody obeys.
lore.extendedMeditation: Éris exposes something unusual about Greek religious thought: its willingness to personify what it disapproved of. She has essentially no cult — no sanctuary, no festival, no priesthood — yet the poets cannot write a war without her. Hesiod's two Erises show the tradition arguing with itself: strife is the curse of mankind and, simultaneously, the condition of every human excellence, for without rivalry the potter never improves his pot. The apple myth extends the insight into politics: the quarrel was not caused by wickedness but by a superlative, by the mere existence of 'fairest' among three goddesses. To the Greeks, Éris was less a villain than a diagnosis — the recognition that conflict is not an interruption of the cosmic order but one of its permanent residents, daughter of the Night that precedes all things.
lore.archaeology: Éris is the rare Olympian-circled figure with no attested temple, sanctuary, or cult anywhere in the Greek world — her existence is literary, and that absence is itself the archaeological fact. Her iconographic life is confined almost entirely to Judgment of Paris scenes: Pausanias (5.18–19), describing the Archaic chest of Cypselus at Olympia, records the wedding of Peleus and the judgment episode in which Éris and her golden apple were among the oldest identifiable figures of Greek myth in art. Roman Discordia survives mainly as the poets' personification; no temple of Discordia is recorded in the city of Rome.
